summaries.body: An operating system manages hardware, mediates between users and hardware, and provides an environment in which programs work.

The operating system aims to execute user programs, make problem solving and system use convenient, and use hardware efficiently. The lecture notes that operating systems appear in devices ranging from cars and phones to personal and enterprise computers.

The kernel is the program running at all times; system programs ship with the operating system but are outside the kernel, while application programs are not associated with the operating system. This common definition avoids treating everything shipped by a vendor as kernel code.

A computer system is organized into hardware, the operating system, application programs, and users. Hardware supplies CPU, memory, and I/O resources; the OS coordinates them; applications use them to solve user problems; and users may be people, machines, or other computers.
The print example gives a dynamic view: a user request travels through application and operating-system components toward the hardware needed to produce output.

summaries.body: CPUs, device controllers, shared memory, internal registers, and drivers cooperate to execute instructions and move I/O data.

One or more CPUs and device controllers connect through a common bus to shared memory. CPUs and devices can operate concurrently and compete for memory cycles, so a memory controller synchronizes access.

MAR identifies the memory address for a read or write, while MBR carries data being written or receives data being read. I/O AR identifies a device, and I/O BR exchanges data between an I/O module and the processor.

An instruction cycle contains fetch and execute stages. PC holds the address of the next instruction and is incremented after each fetch; memory locations contain bit patterns interpreted as instructions or data.

A device controller manages a device type through local buffers and registers. The CPU transfers data between main memory and controller buffers, while a device driver manages controller interaction and presents a uniform interface that hides controller differences from the kernel.

terms.definition: Memory address register specifying the address for the next memory read or write.
Memory buffer register holding data written to or read from memory.
OS software that manages a controller and gives the kernel a uniform interface.

An interrupt saves state before executing its handler.
The vector maps an interrupt number to a handler address.

summaries.body: Interrupts let devices notify the CPU asynchronously and transfer control through an interrupt vector to an interrupt service routine.

Polling makes the CPU repeatedly inspect controller status and busy-wait, reducing utilization. A hardware interrupt instead lets a controller signal that an operation completed or requires attention, which is valuable because I/O devices are often slower than the processor.

On an interrupt, the processor finishes the current instruction, saves minimal state such as PC and registers, and transfers to an interrupt handler or ISR. The interrupt vector table holds handler addresses and is indexed by a unique interrupt number.

The interrupt service routine performs the needed service and then the CPU resumes the interrupted computation. With interrupt-driven I/O, the processor can execute other instructions while the device works, although a long operation can still make a later I/O request wait.

Hardware checks the interrupt-request line after each instruction. An interrupt stage is therefore added after instruction execution so the processor can detect a signal and initiate the proper handler.

terms.definition: A mechanism that changes normal processor sequencing so an event can receive attention.
Interrupt service routine that handles a particular interrupt.
An indexed table containing addresses of interrupt service routines.

summaries.body: Multiple interrupts can be processed sequentially by disabling new interrupts or nested according to priority.

If interrupts are disabled while a handler runs, later requests remain pending until interrupts are enabled again. This strict sequential order is simple but ignores relative priority and time-critical needs.

A priority scheme permits a higher-priority interrupt to interrupt a lower-priority handler. The printer, disk, and communication-line example assigns increasing priorities and illustrates nested control transfer over time.

recaps.body: User goals depend on the device and interface.
The system view emphasizes allocation and control.
The OS must regain processor control after relinquishing it.

summaries.body: User priorities vary by system type, while the system view treats the OS as both resource allocator and control program.

Dedicated workstation users emphasize convenience, performance, and security; shared systems must serve many users; mobile systems emphasize usability and battery life; and embedded systems may run with little or no interface.

From the system view, the OS allocates CPU time, memory, storage, and I/O among competing requests efficiently and fairly. As a control program, it manages execution and I/O to prevent errors and improper use, such as an invalid memory access.
The OS itself is processor-executed software that frequently gives up control and depends on processor mechanisms to regain it.

terms.definition: The OS role that assigns resources among programs and users.
The OS role that manages execution and I/O to prevent errors and improper use.

examTips.body: For hierarchy questions, track the direction of speed, capacity, access time, and cost per bit.

examples.body: Moving from cache toward disk increases capacity and access time while decreasing cost per bit.

mistakes.correction: It is typically volatile and too small for permanent storage of everything needed.

summaries.body: Primary, secondary, and tertiary storage differ in access, persistence, speed, capacity, cost, and typical use.

Registers, cache, and main memory are primary storage. Main memory is CPU-accessible, random access, and typically volatile; it is too small and volatile for permanent storage. Secondary storage extends it with larger nonvolatile capacity but is slower.

NVM devices are nonvolatile and faster than hard disks, while tertiary media such as tape and CD-ROM serve slow, large, special-purpose uses such as backups. HDD surfaces are divided into tracks and sectors.

Storage is hierarchical by speed, size, cost, and volatility. Smaller, faster memory is closer to the CPU; moving downward lowers cost per bit, raises capacity and access time, and reduces processor access frequency. Caching copies information to a faster level.

terms.definition: Storage such as main memory that loses contents when power is removed.
Copying information into a faster storage system.
Slow, large storage used for special purposes such as backup.

examTips.body: Bulk block plus one interrupt points to DMA; repeated status checks point to programmed I/O.

examples.body: DMA lets the disk controller transfer a block directly to memory while the CPU performs other work.

mistakes.correction: The processor still executes transfer work and the interrupt handler; DMA removes per-transfer CPU involvement.
mistakes.misconception: Interrupt-driven I/O removes all processor participation in data transfer.

recaps.body: Programmed I/O busy-waits.
Interrupt-driven I/O still uses CPU instructions for transfer.
DMA transfers blocks directly and interrupts once per block.

summaries.body: The three I/O techniques differ mainly in how much waiting and data movement the processor performs.

Programmed I/O makes the processor issue a controller command and poll status until completion, creating busy waiting and low utilization. Interrupt-driven I/O lets the processor do other work until the controller signals readiness, but the processor still transfers data and runs a handler.
DMA addresses bulk transfer overhead. A controller moves a whole block directly between its buffer and main memory without CPU intervention, producing one interrupt per block rather than per byte.

With DMA, the CPU starts the transfer and is involved again at completion, while doing other work during the transfer. This makes DMA more efficient than programmed or interrupt-driven I/O for high-speed block movement.

terms.definition: I/O in which the processor polls controller status and manages the transfer.
Direct block transfer between a device controller and main memory without CPU involvement in each data movement.

examTips.body: Distinguish multicore on one chip, SMP peer processors sharing memory, NUMA local/remote memory, and clustered networked nodes.

examples.body: Scheduling a process near its allocated NUMA memory reduces remote-interconnect latency.

mistakes.correction: Only general-purpose processors that run processes determine this category; device controllers have limited instruction sets.
mistakes.misconception: Any special-purpose controller turns a single-processor computer into a multiprocessor.

recaps.body: Device-specific processors do not make a system multiprocessor.
SMP processors are peers.
NUMA scales local memory but penalizes remote access.
Clusters use networked nodes for availability or performance.

summaries.body: System categories distinguish general-purpose processors, cores, memory placement, coupling, and availability behavior.

A single-processor system has one general-purpose CPU core even if device-specific processors exist; those limited processors do not run user processes. Multiprocessors use two or more processors and can improve throughput, economy of scale, and reliability.

Asymmetric multiprocessing assigns tasks under a master processor, while SMP makes processors peers that perform all tasks and share physical memory. Multicore puts multiple cores on one chip, improving communication speed and power use; the OS sees N cores as N CPUs.
NUMA gives each CPU fast local-memory access in one physical address space but adds latency for remote memory. OS scheduling and memory management can reduce the penalty.

A cluster links separate nodes over a network and is loosely coupled. Asymmetric clustering uses a hot standby; symmetric clustering runs applications on multiple hosts that monitor one another, using more available hardware.

terms.definition: Symmetric multiprocessing in which peer processors perform all tasks and share physical memory.
A shared-address-space design with fast local and slower remote memory access.
Several networked computer-system nodes working together.

Apply dual-mode and timer mechanisms to operating-system protection scenarios.
Distinguish programs, processes, threads, concurrency, and process-management responsibilities.

examTips.body: Startup order: firmware bootstrap, initialization, kernel load, daemons, services.

examples.body: A software error such as division by zero generates an exception or trap that transfers control to the OS.

mistakes.correction: It is stored in nonvolatile firmware and runs before it loads the kernel.
mistakes.misconception: The bootstrap program is loaded from volatile main memory after the kernel starts.

recaps.body: Bootstrap initializes hardware and loads the kernel.
Daemons can provide services outside the kernel.
Hardware and software events drive OS operation.

summaries.body: Firmware bootstrap code initializes hardware, loads the kernel, and leads into an interrupt-driven running system.

At power-up or reboot, a bootstrap program in nonvolatile firmware initializes CPU registers, controllers, and memory, locates the kernel, loads it into memory, and starts it. The kernel then starts long-running system daemons and provides services.

After boot, the OS waits for events signaled by hardware interrupts or software exceptions and traps. A system call is a user-program request that uses a software-generated control transfer to obtain an OS service.

terms.definition: Firmware code that initializes the system and loads the kernel.
A user-program request for an operating-system service.

examTips.body: For utilization, divide CPU execution time by the complete execution-plus-wait cycle.

examples.body: One microsecond of CPU execution divided by 31 total microseconds equals about 3.2% utilization.
examples.title: Utilization calculation

mistakes.correction: On one core, the OS interleaves jobs by switching when one waits.
mistakes.misconception: Multiprogramming means the CPU must execute all jobs at exactly the same instant.

recaps.body: Uniprogramming idles during process I/O waits.
Multiprogramming keeps several processes in memory.
Job switching raises CPU utilization.

summaries.body: Multiprogramming keeps several jobs in memory and switches away from a waiting job to improve CPU utilization.

A non-multiprogrammed system holds one user process; when it waits for I/O, the CPU is idle. In the numerical example, 1 microsecond of execution in a 31-microsecond cycle yields only 3.2% CPU utilization.

Multiprogramming keeps a subset of jobs in memory, selects one through job scheduling, and switches to another when the current job waits. As long as one process can execute, the CPU need not remain idle.
The timing diagrams compare one, two, and three programs and show how their run and wait intervals can be interleaved.

terms.definition: A program in execution.
Keeping multiple jobs available so the CPU can switch when one waits.

examTips.body: Interactive short quanta indicate time sharing; long I/O waits with job switching indicate multiprogramming.

examples.body: While one process waits for user typing, the OS rapidly switches the CPU to another ready process.
examples.title: Slow keyboard input

mistakes.correction: Batch aims to maximize processor use; time sharing aims to minimize response time.
mistakes.misconception: Time sharing and batch multiprogramming have the same principal objective.

recaps.body: Time sharing targets interactive response.
CPU scheduling selects among ready jobs.
Virtual memory allows programs larger than physical memory.

summaries.body: Time sharing extends multiprogramming with rapid switching for interactive users and relies on scheduling and memory management.

Time sharing switches jobs frequently enough for interaction, targets response under one second, and shares short CPU quanta among users. Batch multiprogramming maximizes processor use, whereas time sharing minimizes response time.

Interactive input operates at human speed, so the OS switches to another process instead of idling. CPU scheduling selects among ready jobs, and swapping moves processes when they do not all fit in memory.

Virtual memory permits processes that are not completely resident and lets programs exceed physical-memory size. Multiprogrammed systems also require file/storage management, synchronization, communication, and deadlock handling.

terms.definition: A short burst of processor time allocated to an interactive job.
A mechanism that permits execution when a process is not completely in physical memory.

examples.body: A timer counter reaches zero and interrupts a user process that never voluntarily returns control.

mistakes.correction: Only controlled events such as a system call, trap, or interrupt transfer control to kernel mode.
mistakes.misconception: A user program can directly set the mode bit to kernel mode.

recaps.body: System calls transfer execution into kernel mode.
User code cannot execute privileged instructions.
The timer prevents indefinite CPU control by one process.

summaries.body: Hardware mode bits, privileged instructions, traps, and timers preserve OS control and protect system resources.
User mode uses mode bit 1 and kernel mode uses 0. A system call changes execution to kernel mode, and return resets it to user mode; interrupts and traps also transfer control to kernel mode.

Privileged instructions such as I/O control, timer management, interrupt management, and switching to kernel mode cannot execute in user mode. An illegal attempt traps to the OS, while protected memory remains inaccessible to user code.

Before running a user process, the OS sets a timer through a privileged instruction. The hardware decrements a counter and interrupts at zero, allowing the OS to regain control from an infinite loop or process that exceeds its allotted time.

terms.definition: Hardware state distinguishing user mode 1 from kernel mode 0.
An instruction executable only in kernel mode.
A protection mechanism that interrupts after a configured period so the OS regains control.

Resources are reclaimed after termination.

summaries.body: A process is an active executing program that owns resources; threads divide its execution, and the OS manages their lifecycle and coordination.

A program is passive, while a process is active and receives CPU, memory, I/O, files, and input while running. Termination requires reclaiming reusable resources; processes may run concurrently on one core or in parallel across cores.

A single-threaded process has one program counter, while a multithreaded process has one per thread. OS duties include creation, deletion, scheduling, suspension, resumption, synchronization, communication, and deadlock handling.

terms.definition: An independent, lightweight execution unit within a process.
Potential execution by multiplexing processes on a single CPU core.

mistakes.misconception: Caching begins by reading the hard disk every time.

Files abstract physical storage properties.
Cache lookup starts at the faster level.
Coherency preserves the latest value across CPU caches.

summaries.body: The OS tracks and allocates memory, abstracts files, schedules disk requests, and maintains useful copies across the storage hierarchy.

Memory management tracks usage, allocates and deallocates space, and decides what processes and data move in or out. File management presents a logical file abstraction over devices, organizes directories, controls access, maps files to storage, and supports backup.

Mass-storage management covers partitioning, mounting, free space, allocation, disk scheduling, and protection. Mounting makes a file system available; scheduling orders queued requests because a disk controller serves one at a time.

Caching checks faster storage first and copies missing information upward from main memory or disk. When a value exists in disk, memory, cache, and registers, updates must propagate; multiprocessors require cache coherency so CPUs see the current value.

terms.definition: Making a file system available to the system and users.
Hardware support ensuring CPU caches contain the most recent shared value.

examTips.body: Access authorization points to protection; attacks and compromised credentials point to security.

mistakes.correction: A protected system can still suffer attacks or misuse through stolen credentials.
mistakes.misconception: Adequate protection guarantees complete security.

recaps.body: Protection regulates access.
Security addresses attacks and stolen authentication.
IDs and groups support access decisions.

summaries.body: Protection controls authorized resource access, while security defends the system against internal and external attacks.

Protection regulates process and user access to files, memory, CPU, and devices. Address hardware confines a process, a timer eventually returns CPU control, and device-control registers remain inaccessible to users.

Security handles threats that protection alone cannot prevent, such as stolen credentials, viruses, worms, and denial of service. User IDs and group IDs associate identities with files, processes, and threads; privilege escalation changes the effective identity for additional rights.

terms.definition: Mechanisms controlling authorized access to OS-defined resources.
Defense against internal and external attacks.
Changing to an effective identity with additional permissions.

examTips.body: Host, VMM, and guest are three distinct roles.

examples.body: A macOS host can use a VMM to run a Windows guest and its applications.

mistakes.correction: The VMM runs and manages guest operating systems while protecting them from each other.
mistakes.misconception: A VMM is itself the guest operating system.

recaps.body: Virtualization hosts multiple OS environments on one machine.
Distributed systems link separate computers.
Network OS nodes remain more autonomous than distributed-OS nodes.

summaries.body: Virtualization creates isolated OS execution environments on one machine, while distributed systems network separate computers to share resources.

A VMM abstracts CPU, memory, and storage into guest environments, runs guest operating systems, manages their resources, and protects guests from one another. A host OS can therefore run applications built for a guest OS.

Distributed systems connect separate, possibly heterogeneous computers to improve speed, functionality, availability, and reliability. TCP/IP is the common protocol, and LAN, WAN, MAN, and PAN classify networks by node distance.

A network OS leaves computers autonomous while enabling file sharing and message exchange. A distributed OS coordinates more closely and presents the illusion of one operating system controlling the network.

Process control covers create, terminate, load, execute, wait, signaling, memory allocation, dumps, debugging, and locks. File and device management provide create/open/read/write/reposition/attributes plus device request, release, attach, and detach.

Information maintenance transfers time, system data, attributes, and debugging data. Communications creates connections and uses message passing or shared memory; protection gets or sets permissions and allows or denies user access.

User goals include convenience, learnability, reliability, safety, and speed; system goals include ease of design, implementation, maintenance, flexibility, reliability, correctness, and efficiency. Hardware and system type influence specifications.

Policy states what should be done, while mechanism states how. A timer is a CPU-protection mechanism; selecting its duration is policy. Separation allows policy changes without redesigning the mechanism.

Modern systems mix assembly at low levels, C in the main body, and C++, scripting, or shell languages for system programs. Higher-level languages improve compactness, debugging, development speed, and portability but may reduce speed and increase storage needs.

summaries.body: Monolithic kernels favor fast in-kernel communication, while layers enforce lower-level dependencies for modular construction and debugging.

General-purpose systems are divided into components with defined functions and interfaces. A monolithic kernel places kernel functionality in one static binary and address space; original UNIX separates system programs from a kernel between system-call interface and hardware.
Monolithic design is simple and fast with little call-interface overhead, but combining many functions makes implementation and extension difficult, and a change can affect distant parts.

A loosely coupled system limits component effects. In a layered OS, layer 0 is hardware, layer N is the user interface, and each layer uses only lower-level services. Construction and debugging are simpler, but defining layers is difficult and traversal overhead harms performance.

summaries.body: Microkernels move services to user space, modules extend a kernel dynamically, and hybrid systems combine structures to balance competing needs.

A microkernel keeps minimal process and memory management plus communication in kernel space, moving nonessential services to separate user processes. Clients and services exchange messages through the microkernel.
Microkernels are easier to extend and port and can be more secure and reliable because less code runs in kernel mode; user/kernel message communication adds performance overhead.

Loadable kernel modules keep core components and link services at boot or run time through known interfaces. They resemble layers but allow modules to call one another, and resemble microkernels without message-passing overhead; Linux uses them for drivers and file systems.
Linux combines monolithic and modular traits. Hybrid systems such as Linux, Windows, and macOS combine models to address performance, security, and usability rather than adopting one pure structure.

A multistage BIOS boot starts firmware code, loads a boot block from a fixed disk location, and uses that code to load the remaining bootstrap and kernel. Modern UEFI provides a single complete boot manager with better 64-bit and large-disk support and faster startup.

The bootstrap can diagnose CPU, memory, and devices; initialize registers, controllers, and memory; load the kernel; and mount the root file system. Only after these steps is the system considered running.

summaries.body: Priority scheduling selects the highest-priority process; under the lecture convention, the smallest integer is highest, and equal priorities use FCFS.

A claim edge records a possible future request and becomes a request edge when a process asks. Assignment changes the request edge direction, and release restores an assignment edge to a claim edge.

summaries.body: Banker’s algorithm uses declared maxima and a safety check before committing a request.

For multiple resource instances, each process declares its maximum use. Available records free instances, Max records maximum claims, Allocation records current grants, and Need equals Max minus Allocation.

The safety algorithm starts Work at Available and chooses an unfinished process whose Need is no greater than Work, then adds its allocation. A request first must be no greater than Need and Available; the system tentatively updates state and restores it if unsafe.

summaries.body: When prevention and avoidance are absent, detection and recovery can respond after deadlock occurs.

For a single instance of each resource type, a wait-for graph has processes as nodes and an edge Pi to Pj when Pi waits for Pj. A cycle exists if and only if the system is deadlocked in this single-instance setting.
The wait-for graph is obtained by removing resource nodes and collapsing corresponding request and assignment edges. Detecting a cycle takes O(n squared) operations for n vertices.

summaries.body: Multiple-instance detection uses Available, Allocation, Request, Work, and Finish rather than a wait-for graph.

The wait-for graph does not apply when a resource type has several instances. Available is a vector, while Allocation and Request are n by m matrices; Request[i][j] is the additional amount Pi requests.

The detection algorithm begins Work at Available and marks a process finished initially only when its allocation is zero. It then reclaims an eligible process’s allocation optimistically; unresolved false Finish entries identify deadlocked processes.

summaries.body: The example changes from a nondeadlocked sequence to a deadlock involving four processes after P2 requests C.

With the original request matrix, P0, P2, P3, P4, P1 can all reach Finish true, so the system is not deadlocked. Adding P2’s request for one C leaves P1, P2, P3, and P4 deadlocked after P0’s resources are reclaimed.

Frequent detection responds sooner to likely deadlocks but costs computation time, especially if invoked for every immediately ungrantable request. Defined intervals are a cheaper alternative and rollback returns a preempted process to a safe state.

summaries.body: Recovery can terminate processes or successively preempt resources, with cost, rollback, and starvation trade-offs.

Termination can abort all deadlocked processes or abort one at a time until the cycle disappears. The all-at-once method clearly breaks the cycle but may discard long computations; one-at-a-time selection considers priority, work, resources, and interactive status to minimize cost.

Resource preemption selects a victim, rolls the victim back, and avoids starving a process repeatedly chosen as victim. A total rollback aborts and restarts the process when determining a safe state is difficult.

terms.definition: Successively taking resources to break a deadlock cycle while addressing victim selection, rollback, and starvation.

summaries.body: Base-limit protection and staged binding separate program addresses from their eventual memory placement.

Only registers and main memory are directly accessible general-purpose storage for the CPU. Base and limit registers restrict a user process to its legal address range; for base 300040 and limit 120900, the inclusive legal range ends at 420939.

Source addresses are symbolic, compilers make relocatable addresses, and linkers or loaders bind them to absolute addresses. Binding can occur at compile time, load time, or execution time; execution-time binding needs hardware address maps.

summaries.body: The MMU dynamically maps the user’s logical view into physical memory when execution-time binding is used.
A logical address is generated by the CPU, while a physical address is seen by the memory unit. They are the same with compile-time and load-time binding but differ with execution-time binding.

The MMU adds the relocation register to a logical address after checking the limit. With base 14000, logical location zero maps to 14000 and location 346 maps to 14346; the user program continues to see its logical values.

summaries.body: Contiguous allocation places each process in one continuous section and manages changing holes.
Contiguous allocation typically keeps the resident operating system in low memory and user processes in high memory. Each user process occupies one contiguous memory section.

Variable partitions create holes of various sizes as processes arrive and leave. Adjacent free partitions are merged, and first fit chooses the first adequate hole, best fit the smallest adequate hole, and worst fit the largest.

External fragmentation has enough total space but no contiguous block, while internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated partition. Compaction requires dynamic execution-time relocation; segmentation instead models a program as logical units such as procedures, stacks, and arrays.

summaries.body: Paging maps same-sized logical pages to physical frames and uses page number plus offset for translation.

Paging divides physical memory into fixed-size frames and logical memory into same-size pages. It avoids external fragmentation but retains internal fragmentation, and each process needs a page table after enough free frames are found.

A logical address has page number p and offset d. For 64 pages of 1024 words mapped to 32 frames, logical addresses need sixteen bits and physical addresses need fifteen bits; a 32-bit logical space with 4 KB pages has two to the twentieth page-table entries.

summaries.body: PTBR, PTLR, TLBs, protection bits, and shared pages support practical paging.

The PTBR points to a page table and the PTLR gives its size. Without a TLB, each data or instruction access needs one memory access for the table and one for the data; a TLB caches translations for faster lookup.

Protection bits define allowed frame access, while a valid-invalid bit says whether a page is in the process logical address space. Read-only reentrant code can be shared, as the libc example maps three processes to one physical copy.

summaries.body: Swapping moves memory images or pages between memory and backing store under memory pressure.
Standard swapping temporarily moves a process to backing store and later brings it back, allowing physical memory to be oversubscribed. Transfer time is proportional to the amount of memory swapped.

Modern systems generally avoid whole-process swapping because it is too slow, but modified page-level swapping is common. A page out moves a page to backing store and a page in performs the reverse operation.

terms.definition: An operation that moves a page from memory to backing store.

summaries.body: Virtual memory runs processes that are not fully resident and demand paging loads pages only when referenced.

Virtual memory separates logical from physical memory, allowing a logical address space larger than physical memory. A process virtual space usually starts at zero, while its assigned physical frames need not be contiguous.

Demand paging brings a page in only when needed. A valid-invalid bit marked i means not in memory and causes a page fault; the operating system checks validity, finds a frame, schedules page-in, marks the page v, and restarts the faulting instruction.

terms.definition: Loading a page into memory only when program execution references it.
